title: Recall: the page always comes back
subtitle: One ledger for every change, and how we test it.
lead: Fizlet runs on someone else's page, so it has to be able to leave. Every change it makes to the page goes through one ledger, and `destroy()` puts back everything the engine still owns, newest first. The DOM then matches a snapshot taken before the engine started. A newer edit by the page always wins.

body.text: The ledger knows five kinds of change, and the engine makes no others. `text(node, value)` sets a text node's value. `style(el, prop, value)` sets one inline style property. `attr(el, name, value)` sets or removes an attribute. `cls(el, name, on)` adds or removes a class. `add(node)` records a node the engine put on the page.

Each records the original the first time it touches something, and what it wrote each time after. `restore()` walks that record backwards. A style attribute comes back byte for byte, not just the same property values.

items: **Change-only.** Writing the value that is already there touches nothing. A browser test writes the same values twice and counts zero DOM mutations; the HUD's test counts 0 mutations over 120 frames where nothing changed.
**Host wins.** If the page changed something after the engine did, the ledger stops writing it and never restores over it. The write returns `false`, so a brick can tell.
**One signal.** Every listener and observer an engine adds is bound to one `AbortSignal`. `destroy()` aborts it, so nothing is left listening.

items.title: The page as the board
items.body: `fizlet/board-page` turns a shot word's letters into 0s and 1s by writing into the page's own Text nodes with `ledger.text`: no wrappers, spans or clones. Recall gives every word back, byte for byte.

items.title: Timelines
items.body: `fizlet/timeline` writes keyframe values through the ledger. Its browser test destroys a timeline mid-play on an element with its own inline style, and the style comes back byte for byte.

items.title: Things the engine adds
items.body: The touch pad, the perf overlay and the match overlay each add one element through the ledger, so `engine.destroy()` removes them too. The perf test checks the host is back byte for byte.

items.title: Slots
items.body: `fizlet/slot` mounts a scene in its own contained stage inside an Astro slot; `destroy()` puts the slot back exactly as the page drew it.

body.text: A reload throws away the visitor's state: their scroll, their form fields, whatever the page's own code was doing. Recall undoes only what the engine did. That is what lets a game knock a page's headings around, or a hero take over a section, and leave it as the visitor left it.
You can try it on the home page: blast the little page, then press **Recall**. That key runs `engine.ledger.restore()`, the same call `destroy()` makes.

items.q: What if my own code writes the DOM?
items.a: Then the ledger doesn't know about it and can't give it back. Write through `engine.ledger` in `render`, or use a brick that does.

items.q: Can I restore without destroying the engine?
items.a: Yes: `engine.ledger.restore()`. The engine keeps running and the next write records a fresh original.

seo.title: Recall: how Fizlet gives the page back · Fizlet
seo.description: Fizlet writes every DOM change through one ledger: change-only, a newer host edit wins, and destroy() restores the page exactly. How, and how it's tested.
